say: Permit weekly cadence only through a predeclared supply gate—not as a rescue after weak engagement. The unresolved question is whether enough fresh, fully verifiable nearby concerts exist to make daily discovery meaningfully different from rereading a weekly list. The supplied concert receipt gives a time and venue, but does not establish admission details or recurring supply. Proposed next test: before inviting students, define 'nearby' and audit seven consecutive days using fixed search sources and a fixed time budget. Require verified time, location and admission, and count distinct concerts rather than repeated listings. Set a daily gate

uncertainty: How many distinct nearby concerts can be fully verified within a fixed search budget, and how often does genuinely new inventory appear? The supplied receipts do not resolve this.
dissent: Sparse supply need not imply weekly demand: students might value daily last-minute certainty about concerts already listed. The proposed freshness gate could therefore reject a useful daily service; it tests a fresh-discovery proposition, not every possible daily-use proposition.

say: revise: Worth a bounded human-run comparison, not a launch. The route notice supports a transport-change use case, not hotel demand or comprehensive arrival coverage. Narrow the prototype to two hotels and explicitly selected arrival routes. Compare cards against each receptionist's usual replies and direct official-notice lookup. Keep €25/month as an untested… Next real test: Within seven days, with €0 cash spend and at most six total person-hours including participant time, ask two consenting receptionists to compare manually prepared cards with their usual replies on the same ten hypothetical arrival questions each, counterbalancing order.

Compare daily cards with usual replies, direct official lookup and a maintained route sheet before building a dashboard. No contact, testing, payment or implementation has occurred.
